MR. LEBLANC (LAURIER)-CHARGES RESPECTING CONDUCT AS CHAIRMAN OF COMMITTEE ON MISCELLANEOUS ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege because I feel that some hon. members have questioned my integrity on two occasions: The member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) on Tuesday December 4 and the member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) on Thursday December 6. I also wish to point out that such an attack had also been made against me as chairman of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates by the member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dins-dale) on Monday, March 15, 1971.
It should be pointed out that those three members are not regular members of the committee which I chair and consequently are unaware of the rules established by that committee.
Hon. members will agree with me that these three members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition have shown political pettiness and niggardliness in their vicious, violent, scathing, low, sectarian, false, erroneous, malicious, discriminatory, detrimental, pernicious and misleading attack. I can think of other qualificatives, Mr. Speaker, but of course I would not dare use them in the House because I know you would find them out of order. I do not want to follow the bad example set recently in this House by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan).
There are three charges laid against me: first, refusal to recognize hon. members of the official opposition; second, irregular use of an illegal chronometer; third, favouritism toward government members to the detriment of those of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition.
I admit, Mr. Speaker, that on Tuesday, December 4, you gave me the opportunity to explain myself. It seems however that these explanations are not sufficient since the hon. member for Calgary North played another dirty trick on Thursday, December 6.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate and respect the decisions made by Your Honour in each case. However, in order that I may settle once and for all, for my colleagues, the public and my constituents, this question which has been dragging on since 1971, if you rule that this is a prima facie question of privilege requiring a motion, I am ready to suggest that this question be discussed before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, as the hon. member for St. John's East and myself have already suggested.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. LEBLANC (LAURIER)-CHARGES RESPECTING CONDUCT AS CHAIRMAN OF COMMITTEE ON MISCELLANEOUS ESTIMATES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc) has given notice to the Chair of his intention to rise on a question of privilege concerning the circumstances he has mentioned. I remind the hon. member that his notice reached the Chair a bit late.
Still he could have risen after the hour of notice, that is in a few minutes. However, I thought that it would be easier to try and settle the matter immediately. The hon. member for Laurier has referred to the fact that this question was raised a few days ago by another member who suggested that there was a question of privilege which should be referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections. Now the hon. member is suggesting that the matter be studied by another committee of the House. The Chair at that time ruled that there did not seem to be a prima facie question of privilege which should be studied by a committee, and I do not see how I could now change this ruling. The hon. member has referred to certain incidents which occurred in a committee. It has been suggested repeatedly that committee deliberations should not be discussed by the House except in the form of a committee report. I regret, like all hon. members, the difficulties which may come up occasionally, similar to those the hon. member has alluded to, but I see no point in having the deliberations of a particular committee looked into by another one. That, in essence, is the ruling I gave the day before yesterday, I believe, and I see nothing in the circumstances mentioned by the hon. member for Laurier to justify any other decision today.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE OF CANDU NUCLEAR POWER STATION TO REPUBLIC OF KOREA AND BUILDING OF HEAVY WATER PLANT IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to advise the House that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has received from the Korea Electric Company Limited, the national electric utility of the Republic of Korea, a letter of intent to purchase a 600 megawatt CANDU nuclear power station, together with an option for another. This is the second time this year that another country has opted in favour of the Canadian nuclear power system, featuring heavy water moderator, natural uranium fuel and pressure tube reactor. In March the Argentine Atomic Energy Commission chose for Argentina's next nuclear power station a 600 megawatt CANDU offered by AECL and an Italian partner, Italimpianti. Contract negotiations for the Argentine project are in the final stages and are expected to be completed around the end of the year.
Acting on the letter of intent, a team of AECL engineers will go to Seoul this weekend for technical discussions relative to the Korean content of the plant. Another team will follow in January to complete specifications and the scope of supply and to set parameters for pricing the project. The aim is to complete the agreement by March.
I would also remind hon. members of the offer which has been made to the province of New Brunswick, mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his statement yesterday, of federal support for a CANDU nuclear power station in that province. As part of the government's general policy of providing financial assistance to the installation of the first commercial CANDU nuclear plant in each province, the government will also be prepared to extend similar financial assistance to the province of Manitoba just as soon as the provincial utility decides to proceed with such an installation.
The growing acceptance of the CANDU nuclear reactor system both at home and abroad has led to a requirement
December 7, 1973

for a further investment in heavy water production facilities, a question which has been kept before the House by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay).

I would like to announce, therefore, that the government will finance the construction of a new heavy water production plant of 800 tons per year capacity in the province of Quebec near the site of the Gentilly reactor. Once built the new facility should provide the assurance of adequate heavy water supplies both at home and abroad for the following several years.
However, projections indicate that the CANDU nuclear industry will continue to grow with even more heavy water needed in future. The government has decided that when the production of an additional federally financed heavy water plant is required in the next few years to support the nuclear program, such plant should be located at an appropriate site in either Manitoba or Saskatchewan.

speechtext:
I should like to congratulate quite sincerely the Atomic Energy Commission and wish them every success with these two prospective sales which I hope are completed satisfactorily. It will be interesting in due course for the House to be told the terms upon which the sales will be financed. However, I do know something about the dedication of the people involved in promoting the CANDU project in Canada, the way they have strived to make this project a success and the way they have worked to promote sales abroad. I wish them every success in this regard.
I think it is pretty clear that in the coming years Canada will have to depend a great deal on the development of atomic power. Obviously there will be a growing role for the CANDU system within our country and there will of course, be an increased requirement for heavy water to be manufactured in Canada.
One thing we note in this connection is a change in the approach of the government. The initial method was to interest private companies in the building of heavy water plants, the first one being at Glace Bay and the second at Port Hawkesbury. Now the trend seems to be away from that toward the government building these plants directly or through the Atomic Energy Commission. It will be interesting to have an explanation some time of this
Atomic Energy
change and whether it is an indication that private companies like Canadian General Electric and others who in bygone years evinced a great interest in building these heavy water plants have lost their interest or whether the government or the Atomic Energy Commission has decided directly it is in the public interest that these plants be built and owned by the government of Canada. It will be interesting to learn why this change in policy has taken place.
Finally, may I also say, in view of the interest the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) has shown in the matter, that I am pleased to see reference made to the possibility of a heavy water plant being built in either Saskatchewan or Manitoba. I shall not take sides, of course, as between Saskatchewan and Manitoba but simply express the hope that before very long the hon. member for St. Boniface will have a heavy water plant of his own to boast about.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE OF CANDU NUCLEAR POWER STATION TO REPUBLIC OF KOREA AND BUILDING OF HEAVY WATER PLANT IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot claim the expertise in this subject the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) can, for which I thank God. I am interested to note that at the time this announcement is made the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) is absent from the House. According to newspaper rumours, he indicated that if the next plant was not constructed in the western part of the country he might tender his resignation. I am wondering whether that is the occasion for his absence.
On behalf of our party may I say this announcement of additional sales of the CANDU reactor is most welcome. I think the government officials involved in negotiating the sales deserve to be congratulated most sincerely. I welcome also the reference in the minister's announcement to the fact that when it becomes necessary to build a fourth heavy water plant it will be located in the western part of the country in either Manitoba or Saskatchewan. This is a welcome announcement and a necessary step. It is important that all parts of the country participate to a great extent in the development of this technology.
I suggest to the minister that, given the current success in the sales of the CANDU reactor, perhaps it is now time for the government to demonstrate even further confidence in the technology developed by our scientists by taking the plunge and going into production of these reactors with the assumption that we can reduce the relatively high initial cost of these reactors through economies of scale that would be involved in a sort of production line run and that by reducing those costs the potential for external sales of the reactor would increase. If increased foreign sales should not materialize, there is great need for such reactors in the future in this country and their production would not be wasted in any way.
Again I congratulate the government and the officia's involved on making these sales and on having developed a technology which is now finding worldwide acceptance and is making Canada one of the leaders in a new area of technology.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having heard yesterday the Prime Minister state the government's energy policy, and having listened today to the

December 7, 1973
Atomic Energy
announcement by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), I must say that, once again, this seems to be a mini-speech from the throne, inasmuch as this policy statement seems in keeping with the expectations of Canadians and parliamentarians.
We have problems, I know, and the Canadian people are counting on their representatives in the House to find solutions, not 20 years from now, but at this very moment, so that they may stop living in anxiety. Are we really going to run short of energy in one area or another. We must stop thinking that we have in Canada natural resources that we are unable to develop and that we must rely on others.
I have been interested for quite a long time in the matter of heavy water production in Canada. Attempts were made by the federal government, the provincial governments, and even by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), when he was premier of Nova Scotia. If we are to rely on information obtained from scientists, it must be admitted that they recognize today that the failure of the Glace Bay project was due to the poor quality of the water that prevented the end from being achieved.
Today, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has conducted extensive research in this area. I am aware of this because I have always kept in touch with this agency to make sure that they were really working in earnest and to find out whether they were going to recommend to the government to set up a new plant in a suitable location where the climate and the quality of the water would allow a large production at the lowest possible cost, thus enabling nuclear plants to operate at full capacity.
I have always been disappointed, Mr. Speaker, that it was decided to build nuclear plants without a secure supply of heavy water to operate these plants at full capacity.
I have nothing against Russia, but I remember very well that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, to a question I asked him in this House, replied that the slowdown at the Gentilly nuclear plant was due to a shortage of heavy water and the inability of Russia to supply more. Because of this answer, I have kept urging the minister and the government that more research be conducted with a view to sitting up a heavy water plant in Canada which could produce more of it in order to allow our nuclear plants to operate at full capacity.
I kept insisting, Mr. Speaker, that this plant be built in the Montmagny area, in the county of Bellechasse, and as recently as yesterday, I talked with the mayor of Montmagny, Dr. Gaetan Gauthier, to whom I pay tribute because he made representations and worked sensibly with his council members, along with his committee, in order to secure a heavy water plant in the Montmagny area.
Today, I must admit that the decision made by the cabinet was a sound one in the light of the information given to me by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. At any rate, I am glad that this plant is located in the province of Quebec. I am a Canadian but I am also a Quebecker. I read in the minister's statement that the government is considering the installation of another plant in a not too distant future in another area of Canada. I think, Mr. Speaker,
that this is the proper procedure in order to bring Canadians closes together instead of dividing them and to enable Canada to benefit fully from all our forms of energy, so that we may work together to solve problems and meet the needs of all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that you are anxious that I complete my remarks. I will conclude right away but, in any case, I hope that the Minister of Energy, Mines, and Resources will continue to show great energy and that this plant will operate as soon as possible, so that we may be self-sufficient and produce all the energy we can in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Previously the minister had indicated that the price freeze on Canadian crude would terminate at the end of January and the Prime Minister had said on national television that the price freeze on Canadian crude in its present form would end in January. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):

subtopic: CANADIAN CRUDE OIL-REASON FOR EXTENSION OF PRICE FREEZE-JUSTIFICATION FOR HIGHER PRICES PAID BY EASTERN CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman will have been aware of widespread disagreement on the question of the pricing of Canadian produced oil in Canadian markets, both within this House and, indeed, on the part of a number of provincial governments. It seemed to us appropriate, in light of the forthcoming first ministers' conference, that this is the kind of question that should be focused on nationally and on which we should seek to get some national agreement. On that basis it seemed reasonable to postpone the date for future increases until we have some agreement with regard to the current position and also with regard to a pricing mechanism for the future, to be discussed within the framework of a first ministers' conference.

Is there any justification for the minister and the government continuing the

existence of these two sorts of Canadians? Is there any justification the minister can give for continuation of a policy which imposes the highest prices on those Canadians with the lowest personal incomes?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Mr. Speaker, as I indicated in my statement, it seems that the earliest nuclear reactor in western Canada will be at such time as the Manitoba utility decides that it should bring a nuclear reactor on stream for its purposes. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to resume this debate and congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for his excellent outline of a national energy policy for all Canadians, Canadians
Energy Supplies Emergency Act from every part of this nation. This policy contrasts with the no-policy of the Conservatives, although I must say that the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) attempted to give his view of what the policy should be from the point of view of the board room and was certainly reinforced last evening by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) in this respect. Somehow,
I just cannot believe this is the prevailing view of the whole party, but who knows? I feel that the New Democratic Party has taken too much upon itself in saying that this is its policy. I should like to show that for nearly a year the Canadian petroleum corporation, or as some of us call it the "Oil-Can" had been on the drawing boards and was actually being considered. A very good document was produced in the month of June which refers to most, if not all, the things mentioned by the Prime Minister last night.
This policy is the policy of the Liberal Party and the Liberal Government and we support it to a man. If hon. members will consult Hansard for October 25, they will see that four speakers on the government side-each of us, including the minister-talked about federal involvement in the tar sands. Clearly, we were very concerned that the approach to the tar sands was the approach taken by a commission of the Alberta government, not some group from New York. These are our policies. We stand behind them but welcome the support of the NDP in this respect.
There are three major elements involved in the Prime Minister's speech and involved in a national energy policy. The first has to be an adequate and secure supply of oil and energy. The second has to be a much greater degree of Canadian control. The third is a single fair price adequate to ensure a secure supply. The Prime Minister discussed these elements last night in general. I should like to deal in some detail with certain of them. Let us deal first with the matter of an adequate and secure supply for all Canadians, both in the short-run and in the long-run.
This bill is designed to assist in securing that supply and making sure that all Canadians do not go short and that no one in Canada suffers. The minister has suggested in respect of the short-run that if there is a shortage of 10 per cent a voluntary program would be effective. He outlined suggestions along that line. If the shortage in the east should go up to 25 per cent, then there would be mandatory allotments and beyond 25 per cent there would be rationing. These short-run possibilities are all covered in this bill. It is however the long-run situation which concerns me most. I should like to deal with the long-run supply situation for a few minutes.
According to the Canadian Geological Survey, CGS, in 1972 Canada was considered to have 134 billion barrels of ultimately recoverable conventional crude oil, that is excluding the tar sands or shales. But by 1973, even though we had only used about half a billion barrels, the CGS estimate had gone down to 99 billion. I am only taking a guess, although I have had some consultations and discussions, that by the beginning of this year the figure will be closer to somewhere between 60 billion and 70 billion barrels. So that in the course of two years we have used roughly one billion barrels, the estimated ultimately recoverable quantity has dwindled from about 134 billion to something between 60 billion and 70 billion barrels, about half of what it was before.

We must also consider that when we refer to this figure of 60 billion to 70 billion barrels we are talking about the oil that is available from the western basin, about 15 billion barrels, and about half of that has already been recovered. We can, therefore, reduce this estimated figure of ultimately recoverable oil outside of Alberta to somewhere in the area of 50 billion barrels, not including, as I said before, the tar sands or any shales that may be available. This is conventional crude. The Prime Minister indicated in his speech yesterday, and this was indicated also in the discussions we have had with petroleum geologists, that the bulk of this 50 billion barrels that is still to be recovered comes from very difficult frontier areas.
There have been very disappointing results in terms of exploration discoveries in the past year or two, which brings us to the conclusion that if we are to continue growth we will have to develop the tar sands. By the early 1980's, it is expected we will need something in the neighbourhood of two million barrels of oil a day ourselves, which will be close to three quarters of a billion barrels a year. Therefore, if we arrive at this point in the early 1980's or by the mid 1980's, what we will have to develop are the tar sands. According to the figures that I have seen from CGS, we have in the neighbourhood of 60 billion to 70 billion barrels of accessible mining type tar sands, and quantities that will vary from 200 million to 600 million barrels of so-called "in situ" sands which have to be extracted in a different fashion. The problem with the mining is that the capital investment is very high. It is estimated that to bring out the two million barrels from the tar sands-and it appears likely that Alberta crude will run out in 1980-1985-we will need an investment of about $30 billion.
It is not just a matter of investment but also a matter of time, how fast you can set up a plant. The industry claims that each plant will take a year and a half. If you peruse a study that was carried out by a government appointed committee of some 40 or 50 senior civil servants in the Alberta government-this was not an outside committee but an interdepartmental committee which produced a very fine document-you will find that we may need up to four years to set up one of these plants. So, we do have a serious problem.
I must say that last night I was very disappointed when I heard the statement made by the Hon. Eric Kierans over the CBC which was totally in error. Perhaps all hon. members on the other side were not here during the whole speech of the Prime Minister or may not have heard parts of it because of the enthusiasm of members on this side for the Prime Minister and for his speech, but I would like to repeat what was said twice by the Prime Minister. At one point Mr. Kierans indicated that $40 million was a ridiculous amount of money to cover the cost of the exploration of the tar sands. Certainly, it is a ridiculous amount of money for exploration, but the tar sands need not be explored, they are not like another oil area. We know where the oil in the tar sands is. Mind you, you may want to take samples, but you know where it is. That amount of money is not for exploration. This $40 million is for research, and in that sense it may even be more than necessary. My feeling is that if necessary more will be

added. It is the research into the in situ tar sands so that the oil may be extracted by methods which are not known to the oil industry that require research. That is what the $40 million is for.
I should like to read a short excerpt from the Prime Minister's comments to make sure that everyone has heard what the Prime Minister said. He said:
It will assist and participate in the research and development work necessary to develop an in situ technology for the production of the vast amounts of oil from the oil sands which cannot be extracted by presently known methods. To this particular end, it will invest approximately $40 million over the next five years in co-operation with the province of Alberta and private firms. Should the province of Alberta prefer some other arrangements for carrying on this project, such as an independent Canada-Alberta institute, the government would be quite prepared to discuss it with them.
I like this concept and I think the people of Alberta will like it. The government will be prepared to discuss it with them. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) then questioned the $40 million, and the Prime Minister said:
No. It is $40 million for research.
I think that the CBC and Mr. Kierans should be corrected. It should be pointed out to them that they made a very serious error in commenting on the Prime Minister's statement relative to this policy.
I have dealt at some length with the shortfall, and I have expressed my concern regarding what will happen in the future when there might be greater energy shortages. This contrasts greatly with the attitude of the other parties in the House which do not appear to be concerned about the long-term supply. I am not referring only to the debate in the last two or three days or in the last two or three months. Since we have been here as a parliament we have been listening to the Conservative Party saying that there is unlimited oil, there is no shortage; let us not worry about it.
During the committee meetings, this is the kind of thing we heard. So, I feel that not enough attention has been given to this problem. What is the solution? Of course, we have to find alternate supplies and we have to depend on some world supplies. We have to find other methods of achieving energy sufficiency. But I think the most important area that we have to consider seriously is conservation, and now I would like to deal for a moment with the subject of conservation. We have mentioned short-term conservation, both voluntary and mandatory, such as turning off lights and measures of this kind. This is part of conservation but a serious look at conservation must include other ingredients. It may even include a substantial change in our lifestyle. Possibly we can expect that type of thing in the not too distant future. It certainly means that we have to rationalize things like our transportation system. It does not make sense to have an airplane flying from Toronto to Montreal using six times the fuel per passenger mile that a railway uses. It means that our railways have to develop fast, rapid transportation.
We should also take another look at Pickering airport. In discussions with the President of the CNR he has convinced me that the $400 million to $800 million involved in that project could establish rapid rail trans-
December 7, 1973

portation between Toronto and Ottawa and Ottawa and Montreal.

speechtext: What about STOL?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
We should examine it also. This is part of the problem connected with the over-all transportation system. I am told there is a factor of four to one in the use of fuel by trucks per ton mile as compared with railways. We must also examine the question of private transportation versus public transportation. If there were not so many private cars on our streets there would be more buses, and the. buses would move faster. These are some of the things I think of when I refer to life style.
There is another problem that has to be solved and conservation seems to be the answer. If, by using a magic wand, we could solve all our energy problems tomorrow we would still create a whole series of other problems. Cheap energy means that we use up our resources at a much faster rate, in turn creating other problems. Therefore, the establishment of a conservation board is one of those elements that are important in terms of secure and adequate supply of energy.
The other ingredient of a secure and adequate supply of energy is the delivery system. We must have a secure delivery system. Here, I must admit that this is perhaps the only element of policy that I have seen coming from the Conservative party. Apparently it made this suggestion a part of its policy in 1969, but it was dealt with only in a very "iffy" way during the 1972 election. There seems to be no argument on this matter. If the phrase "secure energy supply" is to mean anything, it means our energy supply will only be secure if the pipeline to be built is built entirely within the boundaries of Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I would advocate that the pipeline be built in three stages. The first stage would start at St. Ignace, about 30 miles from Sault Ste. Marie, where the oil line now runs, and go from Sault Ste. Marie to Montreal. I understand that the distance between St. Ignace and Montreal is somewhat shorter than the distance between Sarnia and Montreal. The cost for tunnelling and laying the line might be slightly higher, but securing the right of way would be relatively simple as most of the land is held by the Crown.
The second and third stages could almost be built simultaneously, although there should be discussion as to which should come first. The second stage would be to run that line from Gretna, Manitoba to Thunder Bay and around Lake Superior to the Sault. In that way we would have a secure line from Manitoba, at the point at which oil now leaves by pipeline to flow through the United States, to Montreal. I think that is absolutely essential in terms of secure energy deliveries.
The third stage, which could be started soon, would be the extension of the line from Montreal to assure a secure supply to the Maritime provinces. This portion of the line would be reversible, so that oil could flow in both directions, and should be built to accommodate other products besides oil. In short, our delivery policy should be such
Energy Supplies Emergency Act that eventually Canada will have a completely Canadian delivery system stretching from coast to coast.
The second element of a national energy policy which the Prime Minister dealt with, and which I think is absolutely essential, is the quick reversal of the present ownership situation. We must get away from 80 per cent or 90 per cent American ownership to a position which is the reverse of that. The quickest way for this to be done-

I am sorry about that. The quickest way for this to be done would be through the Canadian petroleum corporation announced by the Prime Minister yesterday. I am sorry the Alberta members are not here. They should be interested because I think the Canadian petroleum corporation offers a great opportunity for the people of Alberta. The Prime Minister indicated this yesterday, and I would like to say a little more about it today. It offers an opportunity for the independent Canadian producers. These are the people I would like to see supported. Here, I speak of the Canadian producers who are actually exploring, and the Canadian companies which are doing the drilling.
The Canadian petroleum corporation must also assure supplies to independent Canadian retailers, who are now being forced out of business because they cannot get oil from the multinational corporations. It is extremely important that we, as a government, undertake to support these small independents in every way we can. The Canadian petroleum corporation can give that support. Mr. Speaker, I would like to continue after we resume.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we recessed for lunch I was talking about three elements of a national energy policy that the Prime Minister so eloquently laid out yesterday, namely the adequate secure supply, adequate Canadian control and ownership and a single fair price adequate to maintain this supply.
I should like to go back for a moment to a point that has to do with the notion of Canadian control and ownership and the Canadian Petroleum Corporation or "Oil-Can" or whatever it will be called, and to stress the importance that this company will have in its dealings with the Canadian independents. I think this is a group that could very well be in some trouble in terms of price and other factors. One of the important elements in our policy has to be that we will make sure that we support these independents, that we will support the people who are doing the exploration and we will support the people who are doing the drilling, the Canadian companies in that business. We should also make sure that supplies get to the small
8526

December 7, 1973
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
retailer. It is possible that 200 or 300 of them may go out of business in the next six months in Montreal alone if they do not get supplies. It is these people we want to support, to make sure they get supplies and are allowed to remain in a legitimate business even though small. The small business interests will benefit from the Canadian petroleum corporation.
The third element in the policy is the price. I think that we must have, first, a single price, a fair price and a price that is adequate to meet the demands of our supply needs. The single price is the first thing I mention and when I say single price I believe, Mr. Speaker, that there should be one single price across Canada for oil, excluding transportation costs. Perhaps some day if we rationalize our transportation we can include that in our price. At this point, I think we should have a single price; the people from the east and from the west, Alberta and British Columbia, should be paying that single price. It may be that a producing province, in order to equate this with internal problems or to give the people in the province a fair deal, will want a return in some fashion of some portion of the price. I have heard the Premier of Alberta say this is the sort of thing they may want to do, but there has to be a single price across the country.
Point No. 2, Mr. Speaker, is that the price has to be fair. This is the point upon which there is a great deal of concern. The price that is arrived at has to be justified. There is no justification for someone who can produce 100,000 barrels of oil at $3 per barrel being given $6 per barrel for it. There cannot be a windfall effect and this is one thing we must understand, that there should be no rip-off. The price has to be justified. On the other hand, there have to be ways of inducing people to explore and put money into the tar sands and so on. The NDP feels that they are the only ones concerned about a price freeze, but they must remember that on September 5 it was this party which imposed that price freeze.
There are all kinds of things that we can do about pricing, and all kinds of ways to avoid this windfall type of pricing. My own suggestion, and one that I feel strongly about, is that a national marketing board, separate from a Canadian petroleum corporation, should be established. I think it should be separate in the same way that I think it is wise to have the CBC separate from the CRTC. I do not think the regulatory body or marketing board should be governing the corporation that is operating the business. I think a national marketing board is a good way of achieving a single price. It is also a good way of avoiding a rip-off. A national marketing board could buy $3 oil or $4 oil-I guess there is no $3 oil left-it could buy $6 oil and it could buy from offshore. It could commit itself to buying so many hundred thousand barrels a day from the tar sands at $8 or $9 a barrel and it could commit itself to buying offshore and northern frontier oil at $9, $10 or $12 a barrel. In other words, you can have a mix of prices, each price justified by the fact that we need the oil and are meeting costs with a reasonable profit to the people producing the oil. The final price can be a single price which is an amalgam of all these prices. It would be fair and no one would be ripped-off. This objective can be achieved by a national marketing board.

[DOT]	(1410)
I understand that a national marketing board is one of the alternatives available to us. I hope the government takes a very careful look at this possibility. I realize it will not be easy to put such a board into effect. It will be necessary to deal with the province of Alberta which has proposed its own marketing board. Any dealings of this kind must be based on co-operation.
There is no doubt there is concern in Alberta about the rest of Canada. Albertans have a very important resource, and they need some quid pro quo in order to make this kind of deal possible. I suggested a quid pro quo in speeches I made in October and November. It is very seldom we agree, but my suggestion was similar to the one made by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wool-liams) that the quid pro quo might be within the transportation policy.
The Toronto area, the golden horseshoe, is in a position of overgrowth. The mayor of Toronto is visiting places like Thunder Bay, saying that Toronto has had enough growth and suggesting that we take some of it. One of the ingredients of a national policy for redistributing growth must be some kind of equity in the freight rate structure. This must be designed to redistribute the growth.
Alberta has two major industries, oil and ranching and all the smaller industries that flow from them. It could use some diversification. An important quid pro quo could be this transportation policy. There is a great deal of merit in a national marketing board. It can effect a single price, ensure there will be no rip-off, and ensure adequate money will be available for further development and exploration.
In conclusion, I wish to review the points I have made. Our national energy policy must achieve certain things. There must be an adequate and secure supply. There must be enough exploration. Most important, we must develop the tar sands as rapidly as possible. We must have a very active conservation program. There must be a Canadian national pipeline which will eventually stretch from coast to coast. Our energy supplies, particularly oil and gas, should be controlled by Canadians. The vehicle for this will be the national petroleum corporation which must support the industry, including the independents. We must have a single fair price to ensure adequate supplies of oil in the future. With these ingredients, which were announced in the policy statement yesterday, Canadians can be assured that our energy policy is in safe hands and moving in the right direction.
