Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say a few words on such an important bill.
Mr. Speaker, this bill asks such great things of Canadians that it is imperative that we should consider it seriously and take whatever measures are indicated to meet the needs of Canada for oil products and ensure the developments provided for in the bill.
[DOT]	(M20)
In considering this bill, Mr. Speaker, I ask myself the following question: Why did the government wait so long before introducing legislation to set up an energy supplies
December 7, 1973

allocation board responsible for the distribution of our resources according to the needs of the various Canadian regions? It seems to me the government should have shown more foresight before waking up in the very middle of a crisis. It should have been easy to foresee in view of the Arab-Israeli war. But the government was blind.
It was easy to see that things were going well between those two countries. Since the U.S.A. supply Israel with armaments, and Canada is supposed to be one of their accomplices, it was obvious we would eventually have difficulties with regard to our gas and other oil supplies.
This bill causes us to look at the situation not only in Canada but throughout the world. Few people foresee an end to the present acute world-wide oil crisis. And the conflicting news going round on the matter further add to the existing confusion.
In many countries of western Europe, all car traffic is prohibited on Sundays, especially in West Germany, Italy, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Belgium. Great Britain, Finland, Norway and Poland announced further energy conservation measures. According to the latest news, Mr. Speaker, France and Great Britain will be spared an additional 5 per cent cutback in oil supplies that Arab countries intend to apply this month against all countries who oppose their policy in the Middle East.
In the United States, President Nixon announced further restrictive measures prohibiting gas stations from staying open from 9 p.m. on Saturday until midnight on Sunday. Companies will have to reduce their deliveries of liquid fuel to individuals by 15 per cent, to business concerns by 25 per cent and to industries by 10 per cent. Supplies of aircraft fuel have be reduced by 5 per cent and again to 15 per cent starting next month.
Mr. Speaker, as you see, we are in great difficulty and it is high time for us Canadians to take the required steps, inasmuch as it is materially possible and feasible to extend the pipeline and to ensure the development of our natural or oil resources. Supplies from Alberta barely meet Quebec needs.
It has been recalled that we import about 25 per cent of our oil from Near East countries. Moreover, it must be noted that most of our supplies come through the Port-land-Montreal pipeline. Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi may stop providing Montreal refineries with oil carried by the Portland pipeline.
The 25 per cent cutback in Arabian production may result in a 20 per cent decrease in world supplies. Eastern Canada would then feel directly the effects of such a cutback as well as of a world shortage.
Granting, Mr. Speaker, that work volume is comparable to that of previous years, we must anticipate a possible shortage for next year. Because of a possible worsening of the Quebec situation, it is our duty to take the necessary measures to ensure the provision of essential services and also to advocate voluntary consumer restrictions.
With regards to the federal project of extending the pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal, no decision should be made before further meetings between the federal and Quebec governments.
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I regret that Quebec did not see farther than its nose and that it prevented the extension of the Sarnia-Montreal pipeline, in order to promote the building of a deep-sea harbour to import foreign oil instead of encouraging Canadian oil companies.
Mr. Speaker, I blame Quebec's childish policies. If we are short of oil in Quebec and were taken by surprise, the fault lies with the province. The Quebec government persisted in wanting the federal government to build a deep-sea port to get foreign oil, while it would have been preferable to extend that pipeline to Montreal.
Today, we say that if there is a Borden line, the fault lies with Quebec. Quebec could have been provided with a Canadian service that would have been able to provide sufficient supplies to meet the needs of the eastern provinces. In order to develop our resources and sell our oil at reasonable prices, the time had come to take the necessary steps and provide for the financing of that project with Canadian capital and at low interest rates since it is to serve public interest.
We also believe, Mr. Speaker, that the government should issue the development permits it usually grants to companies developing Canadian resources in order to keep certain controls so as to meet with whatever situation might arise. However we regret to see that this legislation is limited to the creation of machinery, without specifying political and economic frameworks, without creating any financing agency, since in those great projects, the "dance of millions" will start, and that will increase the price of money as well as building and production costs. In all their speeches, not one of the previous speakers mentioned finance. Yet, this field is the most important. It is the first one for which we should make arrangements for easy term financing of such gigantic projects.
Mr. Speaker, the important thing is not the price freeze, but the freeze on interest rates. Interest rates are now excessively high and if we go ahead with these big projects we shall have to pay these high interest rates, which will increase construction costs and the cost of living of all citizens.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated yesterday that he would propose measures to cope with that. Since family allowances and old age security pensions are geared to the cost of living increase, the latter will therefore continue to increase to unequaled heights. If the cost of living goes up again, Mr. Speaker, how will the Canadian people survive? How will they pay all those taxes and the excessive interests on money? How can we make both ends meet if we undertake to build what must be built and ensure urgent and essential developments in our country? We should also devise technical means to finance all those projects at very low interest costs, that is the administration costs.
Moreover, the Prime Minister stated yesterday that he would only have to ask the steel makers to produce at cost price. Why does he not ask those who control money and credit to also supply credit at cost price? Because as a good many others he is tied by the neck, a servant of financial magnates. He is not one of those who want to give back to the state what belongs to the state.

December 7, 1973
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
Mr. Speaker, the state must be independent, and the way we are acting now, we are far from being independent. We depend on foreign capital, on those who make capital out of nothing. If we want to develop our natural resources, we will have to ask permission of these servants of financial interests, as if they owned our natural resources.
Everybody says that these natural resources belong to us, that all we have to do is develop them, but in order to do that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), the Prime Minister and the government will have to kneel in front of big finance to ask permission to develop these natural resources. It will be necessary to take the assets of all Canadians, the assets of all new developments and to credit them to this sacrosanct finance.
There, Mr. Speaker, is where we stand. This is how we should work in a logical way. This is where we should put all our activities in order to build what we ought to, make Canadians benefit from their resources and not take them away from them by doing what we do now. Instead of developing our resources for Canadians, we develop them for a few financiers, to their profit at the expense of Canadians. We commit Canadians to pay a tribute for generations and these developments will never be theirs. They will always be the property of those who finance them.
If we want a sovereign government, Mr. Speaker, the time has come, with respect to the great developments that are essential, to assume our financial sovereignty, put it to the test and at the disposal of the Canadian public. The time has come for us to use it to develop our resources and satisfy the needs of Canadians, so that they will secure and, above all, retain the ownership of their assets and property.
Mr. Speaker, in order to bring about the necessary developments, namely, the sharing of Canadian resources with the Canadian people, thereby providing them with the bare necessities of life, we shall have to get even deeper into debt while paying tribute to high finance. Mr. Speaker, we shall be enslaved even more than we are now, because the Canadian debt is astronomical and the interest on the federal debt alone exceeds $3 billion. This debt is huge and unbearable. If we increase the public debt even more through these developments, we will increase interests as well. We will therefore increase taxpayers' interests and taxes to such an extent that they will be compelled to go bankrupt.
The previous speaker said a moment ago that independent companies were going bankrupt, but when this pipeline is built under the present system, all Canada will go under. Mr. Speaker, everything will go into the hands of big financial institutions that exploit to the utmost the economy of countries, in particular that of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I say that this government has carried out a short-range policy and I will prove it in a few moments. As a matter of fact, a large percentage of Canadians have been kept unemployed for several years. Therefore, we could have carried out the developments that were necessary for Canada and provided some work for these people instead of paying them unemployment insurance benefits, instead of taking from those who work in order to give to those who do not work. This is what we could have done.

But the government, with their short-range policy, have always blocked everything. We are always blocked by finance. A lot of projects should have been undertaken but were not because the necessary funds were not available and we were afraid of getting further into debt.
Our financial institutions are there to serve us and had they done just that instead of catering to the few big financial institutions that we know, we might have distributed our resources to the benefit of Canadians and put at their disposal the wealth that exists everywhere in Canada. We will never lack oil or energy products since we are able to develop them. There is plenty of energy and oil products in Canada, but in order to develop them, Mr. Speaker, we have to get into debt for generations to come. Such development should be possible without getting into debt.
New developments require new credit and it should be issued without interest. Mr. Speaker, we could give back our national heritage to the Canadian people, we could leave them their assets instead of merely changing their owners. To hand over undevelopped natural resources in return for credit to finance them is as bad, Mr. Speaker, as giving the neighbour's house to the State or to somebody else.
In order to carry on the necessary developments, Mr. Speaker, namely to distribute Canadian resources to Canadians and look after the bare necessities of life, we will have to go into debt forever.
Under our current system we have all the necessary facilities to give Canadians a sound economy and develop all those major resources and mainly our oil resources. We have all the necessary facilities for their transportation and development. We also have, if we want to take the time to think about it, all the necessary facilities to finance those enterprises without creating new mortgages on old mortgages.
Thus the administration cost would decrease as the debt is amortized and Canadians would become owners instead of have-nots. Under the current system one must be an accomplice and a parasite to give our natural resources to foreigners for developing them. They are being mortaged and in addition to that perhaps we will have to pay them ten times within ten years.
I would like to say a few words about the speech made yesterday by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as reported in today's Le Devoir. I will only quote one excerpt. The Prime Minister stated:
This is why the government has decided to invest $40 million within five years in a research and development project of the Alberta oil sands; this is also why it is prepared to make equity investments in the corporations which will exploit those oil sands as well as in those which will do the same in the Arctic and offshore through the new national petroleum company.
The new national petroleum company has no financial facilities. And to finance it the government will have to find money somewhere. The Prime Minister stated that the government will buy shares in those corporations and financial developments. To buy shares it will need money, and the Prime Minister will do as usual: he will try to sell phares on Canadian market to suck up all the savings of
December 7, 1973

the taxpayers and hand them over to the state that could find other sources of financing.
When the state takes all the available savings, there is nothing left to set up industries, and promote the economic development of Canadians. All government levels, provincial as well as federal and municipal, take hold of the people's savings and invest them on the long term in projects like those that have just been mentioned, while Canadians are without money. No one can invest except the Industrial Development Bank that gouges Canadians, industrials and businessmen by lending them money at exorbitant rates.
Mr. Speaker, the quotation continues as follows:
Among the five main points of the new national oil policy, which is explained elsewhere in detail, the construction of a pipeline to Montreal is perhaps the least spectacular measure, as this decision was announced three months ago; but, according to Mr. Trudeau, it is "by far the single most urgent step towards the achievement of our national goals".
Mr. Speaker, we all agree on that point. This pipeline should have been built long ago. But we know that what is most important is to find the money to build it. If we do not do so, we will build it to the expense of Canadians, and we will involve into debt not only the present generation but generations, to come, and we have no right to do that.
I go on quoting:
Without a pipeline, said the Prime Minister, eastern Canada will never be certain that it can meet its requirements should overseas supply be interrupted.
Moreover, without a pipeline the government is unable to guarantee a market in Canada for Canadian oil at a level sufficient to ensure the development of the oil sands and other Canadian sources of supply.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that this will require once again billions of dollars, and those billions, we will not find in the pocket of a beggar, when there is only about $414 billion in legal money in circulation. According to figures of the Bank of Canada, there are about $4!4 billion in legal money in circulation. Are we going to pay off all our debts with $41/2 billion, when the federal debt amounts to almost $48 billion? Federal, provincial and everybody's debts in Canada exceed $130 billion. We have $4 VS billion to pay them off. Are we going, with $414 billion, to pay for developments that amount to $5, $6, $7 or $8 billion? No figures are available in this regard. These are figures that I submit to the House, but I am quite sure that it will amount to about $10 billion. Only $414 billion in legal money in circulation. Therefore, we will have to issue new credits. Those new credits will be issued through debts, mortgages, repayments. We will have to repay perhaps three or four times more than we received.
This is the assumption, Mr. Speaker. Governments should open their eyes instead of laughing at what we are doing and what we are suggesting. Instead of laughing at the suggestions we made, the implementation of which we long called for, they should keep their eyes and their ears open and try to understand once and for all that it is impossible to develop a country by running it deeper and deeper into debt and by always paying back double or triple the amounts received. It cannot and will not always work. It can work for some time but not always. I keep on quoting:
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
Even though the extension of the price freeze west of the Ottawa Valley until the end of winter smells of political opportunism, the overall position of the Trudeau government on the long term price system effective for the oil industry stays unchanged. Evidently, Mr. Trudeau now agrees with the NDP that for the moment higher prices for Canadian oil would neither be necessary nor justified. On the other hand, he threatens that "this undisputable fact" and "this unpleasant truth" that the era of plentiful and cheap energy has gone.
We want to prevent prices from going up but the problem will not be solved by freezing prices. Prices are frozen and then, as in the United States, they have to be unfrozen, otherwise industries close down. In order to prevent their closing down, prices have to be unfrozen.
What we need, Mr. Speaker, is to adjust prices to the purchasing power. Consequently, prices must be lowered instead of frozen. The economic method we advocate contains a price adjustment mechanism which would also reduce the cost of production and the cost of finance which would allow for cheap production for all Canadians and allow them to live decently in their country which is bursting with wealth. Finally, it would allow for the distribution of that wealth because it belongs to Canadians. It does not belong to a few financiers who never lifted a shovel and never will and who use only their pen to print figures and lend that accounting to the state or large corporations who will be developing the energy we will need to keep Canada operating. This is a banker's pen run country.
The government must take control of that pen and force financiers to issue new credits for new developments at administrative cost. Then, Mr. Speaker, we will be doing something for this country. We can develop everything that is physically possible and normally good to develop. We will never be able to do it otherwise, certainly not by continuing to increase debts, mortgages, the cost of living and setting up a kind of economy where life becomes impossible, governments rip off individuals to pump money in the pockets of high finance. Mr. Speaker, we will have to put an end to this one day.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, debating Bill C-236 on Friday afternoon seems a bit of an anticlimax, having decided which way the vote will go next Monday. I really cannot help but think, in respect of this emergency act, that the government could be accused of using a sledge-hammer to kill a fly. The government has not proven the energy crisis in Canada is severe enough to justify this far-reaching intervention in the rights of the private sector, retailers, wholesalers or of the provinces at the present time. The government has not justified the need for these sweeping powers to deal with the present situation in Canada. We should not be stampeded into giving up all rights as individuals merely to deal with the problem, although it is important, because the net result may well be worse than the problem itself. We have just dealt with the foreign investment bill, and many considered it of little significance, by which the government is going to effectively divest most areas of Canada of what little local control they have.
Before this bill is passed, there should be an intensive inquiry into Canada's energy crisis to determine the true extent of it. We have been told time and time again that

December 7, 1973
Energy Supplies Emergency Act this energy crisis is a crisis of transportation and distribution rather than of production. In the short-run, this is undoubtedly true, but there are many more serious portents in respect of the long-run. I do not think the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) dealt with them adequately yesterday.
We have heard criticisms from the NDP that the decision of the Conservative Diefenbaker government was instrumental in creating the oil shortage by instituting the Ottawa Valley line and not continuing the pipeline to Montreal. Without the creation of the Ottawa Valley line, there would have been no market for western oil except what the United States took, and the western oil industry would not have been developed. There are those who suggest that this policy cost Ontario dearly, an estimated $500 million in ten years. But perhaps to put it in proper perspective, I should remind hon. members that the consumers of Canada will benefit to the extent of $150 million in this year alone by the discounting of wheat and feed grains to the western producers for the benefit of consumers who are mostly in eastern Ontario.
We have heard so many conflicting statements, Mr. Speaker, as to what is the real or expected shortage of supplies that we are entitled to hear from the government exactly what its assessment of the situation is. If there is to be a serious shortage in the Maritimes and Montreal, let the government present its findings and analysis if it has any.
Now, what about the possibility of resumption of supplies of offshore oil. It certainly seems likely that the Arab oil blackmail will be unable to last indefinitely, but it certainly and probably will last for this winter. In assessing the Middle East situation we must realize that Syria and Egypt, the Arab Republic, are now in a very weak position and that the strength of the Arab world has shifted to the monarchies. Jordan hardly joined in the fighting. Certainly, the Arab kings are fearful for their monarchies and really fear the Arab Republics more than they do Israel. They are also aware that they might lose the U.S. market permanently. Indeed, it seems likely that the Arab oil boycott has already set in motion the measures necessary to allow considerable independence from the Arab demands.
We need to know in the short run, what is the situation this bill is designed to cope with; we want to know what powers the government will have and what the objectives are. Can the allocations board be criticized for its lack of independence? There are thousands of products that can be affected by the decisions of the board. No one will oppose a reasonable amount of allocation and regulation if necessary, but the dimensions of the immediate crisis must be made clear.
Mr. Speaker, turning to the longer-term crisis, there are those who suggest that this may well be a turning point in the lifestyle of the people of this continent. The conservationists have made the accusation that the Americans, with 8 per cent of the world's population, are using 33 per cent of the world's energy. Somehow or other, many Canadians accuse the Americans of this, but they forget that we Canadians are in the same position. They forget

also that we are part of the North American continent, and that we cannot escape the fact that if there is a lifestyle change in the United States there will be one for us. Already the stock markets are reacting by the most drastic fall since the great depression and are still on their way down. With about 40 per cent of the North American economy tied to the automobile industry, any drastic change is bound to severely affect our economy.
There are those who suggest that by keeping the price of fuel oils far below world prices we could somehow insulate ourselves from the world prices and still have a prosperous economy. There are those who suggest that by somehow preventing the export of energy, we could have a very cheap supply and could isolate ourselves from the North American economy. Mr. Speaker, surely it is impossible to do this on any more than a short-term basis without doing serious damage to our own energy resources. Keeping the price of oil and gas so low, when it is such a valuable commodity, can only increase the drain on the rather limited supply of cheap oil and gas that is available to our country.
It has always been interesting to me that when a rural family had to accept welfare for some reason, the first thing that the welfare officer did was to have them throw out the woodstove and replace it with an oil burner, on the basis that the family was deprived. Rationing by price is certainly one of the most effective methods of reducing consumption of these very valuable commodities of oil and gas and, if we are seriously concerned about the preservation of these very important commodities, we should allow rationing by price.
If we are concerned about sudden drastic increases causing hardship, we could look at the staging of prices and financial support for the disadvantaged groups. After all, we are doing just this with regard to food. There has been a drastic increase in the price of food, but no one has suggested that we should have a price freeze on food because it is recognized that we need these price increases if we are to have food on the table. Indeed, there are those who suggest that precious oil and gas commodities should not be burned in stoves but should be reserved for the use of the plastic industries and for production of the many products that have enriched the lives of the people of the world. If nothing else, this debate should focus attention on some areas in which our energy needs can be debated.
There is one aspect of this bill, and an aspect of the export tax, that is very disturbing to anyone who thinks seriously of the prospects of Canadian unity. The implementation of the export tax without consultation with the government of Alberta, on a non-renewable resource, is one of the greatest attacks on a region and a province that has been made in this country. First of all, this tax, which may or may not be justified, could not be implemented in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec without their consultation. This is a serious manifestation of what the government of Canada is willing to do in the periphery areas at any time it suits it, on the basis of so-called national interest. It also happens that the government of Alberta is a Conservative government, and therefore this administration felt completely free to inflict any punishment it wished on the people of Alberta. Similarly, under the provisions of this bill the government can
December 7, 1973

extract from the provinces all their resources and thus deprive them of a reason to exist. This situation cannot help but strengthen the feeling that, for western Canada at least, there is not much in the Canadian confederation for them. The government has given the excuse that the oil companies were making windfall profits and therefore the tax was necessary.
Mr. Speaker, in a Finance Committee meeting the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) suggested that out of every dollar of this tax, about 22 cents would have been returned to the producing province and that of the balance, almost 40 cents would have gone to the federal government in corporation tax. Even if the whole dollar were used by the oil companies as profit, with no re-investment, 40 cents would have been returned to the dividend holder but, so if he were a Canadian he would have paid a third, on the average, to the federal treasury.
If companies are making windfall profits, there are many other ways in which they can be taxed. Canada has only ten years supply of conventional crude at the current rate of usage. The rate of discovery in Canada has been disappointingly low, and there has been a net drop in reserves. In the province of British Columbia, under an NDP government, the number of wells drilled in 1973 compared to 1972, dropped from 190 to 138, with Saskatchewan staying almost the same, and only Alberta showing a 50 per cent increase. In recent committee meetings it was pointed out that last year the industry found only 75 million barrels of oil, and the equivalent in gas, for an expenditure of $385 million, which amounts to a rate increase of $5 a barrel.
The Canadian Society of Petroleum Geologists estimates that although our potential reserves amount to 60 billion barrels, significant quantities of oil can only come from one area, namely Newfoundland and Labrador, at $5 to $6 a barrel. It is also pointed out that the 3 million or 4 million barrels of oil that geologists claim lie undiscovered in western Canada either do not exist or represent very high-cost oil. This leaves the tar sands of Alberta and Saskatchewan as the prime sources of Canadian energy requirements. But all indications are that the tar sands oil will be expensive and that it will cost at least $6 a barrel before it could be exploited. Clearly, the price could be much higher.
The development of the tar sands by Syncrude, which holds rights on eight square miles out of the 30,000 square miles of tar sands, will cost upward of $1 billion which will be invested in processes that are not yet completely proven. This is hard to see as a sell-out to multinational corporations, particularly when the Alberta government has begun indexing, which will provide the people of Alberta with a stake in the profit and will ultimately benefit the people of Canada through the transfer of payments.
Almost certainly, the development of the Alberta tar sands will provide Canadians with expensive energy because the project is work-intensive and the costs will rise as the general wage level rises. Furthermore, the project will be competitive with similar projects in the large conventional oilfields around the world, such as the
Energy Supplies Emergency Act one in Alaska and the one in the North Sea where four wells have a proved potential of two billion barrels of oil, and taking into account the Colorado shale sands and coal gasification it is almost certain that Canadians will have to pay a high price for energy if we must rely on the Athabasca tar sands.
The announcement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) yesterday that, in effect, Canada will have to rely on the tar sands as the major source of energy requires a great deal of thought and consideration. All the authorities suggest that the development of the tar sands is an expensive proposition. If it is to be made economic, this fact will have to be recognized by the federal and the provincial governments. Oil from the tar sands will not be cheap oil, and if these governments attempt to ignore the fact it will not be possible to proceed with the development of the resource. It seems certain that significant changes will have to be made in the tax on conventional crude oil, and rather than obtaining more government revenue from the tar sands development lower taxes will have to be applied if the cost of the tar sands project is to be low enough to produce oil at a price competitive with other conventional fuels.
In the eagerness to abolish the export tax it has been forgotten that oil prices are set on the international market and that the price of crude has risen partially in relation to the devaluation of the American dollar. It is certainly analogous to the price of wheat, which has risen from $2 to $5.50 based largely on the devaluation of the American dollar.
I do not see how a widespread differential in oil price on either side of the U.S. Canada border can exist. We would have to curtail or virtually prohibit the entry of American cars into Canada. This would disrupt our tourist trade and it would certainly disrupt the historic pattern of trade between the two countries. Unless we wish to retreat within our borders and cut off the movement of goods and people across the border, we cannot have an effective two-price system. The Americans are attempting to ration their energy through rising prices, and this eventually creates a much better balance even if it has serious effects on certain segments of the economy.
There is another aspect of the oil situation that we should consider carefully. For generations the Maritimes and Quebec have benefited from cheap offshore oil. Almost certainly the historic trend in the development of oil will return when the situation normalizes. The Arab nations will continue to provide a large pool of conventional oil to the world because, whether we like it or not, the world will use the resources collectively.
In Canada we have a dual situation in view of the fact that Quebec represents a relatively independent segment of our nation. For hundreds of years, the French community in the world has been on good terms with the Arab world, as is evidenced by the fact that unlike the situation of the Netherlands and West Germany, France is now enjoying almost normal trade relations because of its exemption from the Arab oil embargo. It has been reported that a similar offer has been made to the province of Quebec and that they may expect sympathetic treatment from the Arabs. Why do we not use this advantage to broaden our contacts with the Arab countries and take
8532

December 7, 1973
Energy Supplies Emergency Act advantage of the special possibilities that exist in this regard?
Yesterday the Prime Minister suggested that Canada would be glad to invest in a Mackenzie Valley pipeline to carry Alaskan and Canadian gas to the south. Investment agents are now advising that the purchase of Mackenzie delta stocks in such companies as Imperial, Shell and Numac are not very attractive because, in the view of many, the chances of success of the Canadian Arctic Gas system are not great. It is believed by many that the Trans-Alaska pipeline will be the carrier bringing North Slope gas to the U.S. market.
The so-called LNG technology is not new; it has been in operation for ten years. It is pointed out that the major disadvantage of the El Paso project, for Canadians, is that it is a U.S. project within the control of the United States. The events of the last six months have made the Americans distrustful of the suppliers of energy. It is widely stated in Washington that the recent pronouncements from Ottawa have caused Washington to be dubious of the sincerity of their northern friends. Some time ago it seemed that the Canadian Arctic Gas group was in a position of advantage, but even they admit that El Paso is a competitive project and that cost will be secondary to security. The Trans-Alaska gas line route is shorter and the Alaskan Indian claims have been settled, while the Canadian Indian claims have not. It is generally agreed that a treaty will have to be drawn up between Canada and the U.S. and that such a treaty is not possible at present in Canada. A study of the merits of the two projects indicates that the Trans-Alaska pipeline would bring great benefits to Alaska and would give it a chance to build a petrochemical complex for the provision of energy to the Pacific rim countries.
If the El Paso project is adopted, it is likely that the Canadian project could not be proceeded with as the amount of gas found in the delta is not sufficient to warrant the construction of a pipeline at this stage. Furthermore, even if the pipeline were to be built some time in the future to fill Canadian needs, the price of gas would have to be much higher than has been foreseen. The major reason for not building the pipeline, in the eyes of the Americans, is national security and their desire to see their project wrapped in the American flag. So that if Canadians feel they should go ahead with the construction of the Mackenzie Valley gas pipeline, a great deal of effort will have to be made at the diplomatic level to bring this about.
It is too bad that the Mackenzie Valley pipeline has not been built, because according to the evidence which was brought forward in the committee the Mackenzie Valley basin is one of the areas where oil exists in small quantities. Without a pipeline to tap it, it does not seem that it will be worthy of development for a good many years yet.
Yesterday the Prime Minister announced a national petroleum company. It is difficult to foresee what will be its role. I took it from the Prime Minister's words that he sees it as an exploration company. But I point out that in the area of conventional exploration, where wild-catting is prevalent, government companies operate the poorest and

private companies operate the best. Manitoba has a government-sponsored mining company which is try-ing to find new mines. It has spent a considerable sum of money and is now being criticized because it has not yet found anything. So far as the tar sands are concerned, these are already discovered. The Alberta government has a stranglehold on production from them, and the profits from the oil sands will eventually become available to all Canadians.
The crux of the problem will be the extent to which Ottawa attempts to control and exploit western Canadian resources for the national good. If this is applied to all resources, eventually we will end up with a unitary state. The complete centralization at Ottawa of all resources would not be good for Canadian unity. If oil resources should be centralized at Ottawa, then a good argument can be made for having all the resources of all the provinces centralized in a similar manner. In a country of so many regions such as ours, this would place a great strain on confederation.
It has been suggested that a single national marketing agency would be valuable in the energy field. The Canadian Wheat Board is an example of a single national marketing agency. It has been very successful in selling grain abroad at as high a price as possible for the Canadian farmers, but when it comes to setting the price of grain within the country it runs into problems. Should it set the price in favour of the producers, or in favour of the consumers? Generally speaking, those with the largest political clout will win out.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae), who spoke earlier this afternoon, said that the proposed Canadian petroleum corporation would help small, independent petroleum producers. I suggest that small businesses find it very difficult to get along with government and government agencies. Large industries, in contract, have a lot of back-up and management and are able to deal with government on a much better basis. The Canadian petroleum corporation, far from increasing the input of small companies, will reduce their input in favour of the much larger companies.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having worked for 25 years in the private sector, I sometimes happen to feel philosophical misgivings when we have to debate bills involving a much more intense activity from the government in the economic affairs of this nation.
When we will have to consider and to evaluate the interests involved and the general good of the Canadian people, I think we will have to offset any inclination we may have towards free enterprise and set our sights on the importance of protecting the Canadian people as a whole. That more or less sums up the problem put to us today in this debate and without hesitating, I must state that, on the issue of energy and oil, I stand left of center. Mr. Speaker, in the face of the insecurity we know here in the area of energy, I do not hesitate to take position in favour of marked and direct action on the part of the federal government in the area of energy in general and oil in particular.
December 7, 1973

Mr. Speaker, that is why Bill C-236, which for all practical purposes aims at giving the federal government extensive powers to administer the supply and distribution of oil in Canada during one year, is a bill we will have to support precisely because it aims at protecting the interests of Canadians as a whole.
I am pleased that this government has deemed necessary to restrict the duration of the bill, since it will expire in a year. If necessary, Parliament may approve an extension of the powers provided in the bill now under consideration.
As a result of the restriction applied under that legislation, I am ready to trust the cabinet as well as the agencies it will establish to cope with the present emergency.
Having said that, I woulk like to review the situation and add a few facts omitted by previous speakers. Canada is producing at the present time some two million barrels of oil per day. Of that amount, about 50 per cent is exported to the United States, while the other 50 per cent is used in Canada from Vancouver to Ottawa.
But in earlier years, the rest of Canada had to depend on offshore supplies. Going back some years, we realize that we began developing energy in Canada in 1947. Prior to that, Canada had been dependent on U.S. imports for western Canada and on Arab imports for eastern Canada.
Until 1947, Mr. Speaker, for all practical purposes, we were not producing a barrel of oil in Canada. It is only in 1947 that we started to develop the resources discovered in Alberta. In the following years, that industry was developed but it was in competition with a very sound and expanding industry in the United States which was competing with the new Canadian industry.
Then in 1961, the Canadian government took a first step and by creating a protected Canadian market for the western industry allowed that industry to develop.
That brings me to discuss the position of the province of Quebec on that issue. Some people wonder what is the position of Quebec in the present crisis, especially on the proposals put forward by both sides.
In the past, as I said, the province of Quebec has always depended on offshore supplies. That has always been true and with a few exceptions, it is still true today. The international market was operating and Montreal was supplied with fuel mostly by tankers, at least during the shipping period. There was also the pipeline which is still in use from Portland to Montreal that served to ensure the supply to a certain extent after the shipping season.
That system worked out quite well through the years but now the market has developed, the demand has increased and the oil shipped from Portland is not enough, especially when the supply may be stopped at Portland.
In 1961, when the Canadian government decided to set the Borden line, it was a sound decision, Mr. Speaker, but yet, at that time, that measure was to a certain extent contrary to the interests of Quebec because the refining industry in Quebec, particularly in Montreal, supplied the Toronto and all the Ontario market, since the tankers were not using the St. Lawrence Seaway to reach the
Energy Supplies Emergency Act United States and the Great Lakes with a sufficient amount of oil.
Over that period Montreal has been able to benefit from the Ontario market and when that decision was taken in 1961, it had a negative effect on the Montreal industry. We from the east and from Quebec in particular accepted it because this was a fair Canadian policy aimed at protecting and allowing the growth of a required Canadian industry.
In Montreal, we experienced for a number of years a freeze on our oil industry which did not grow until 1970, that is nine years later when we witnessed a growth in the field of refining for the province of Quebec.
To a certain extent, therefore, by agreeing to this policy we contributed to rationing at the development level. Obviously we did keep on benefiting from a price which was advantageous for us in the east, in Quebec and in the Maritimes. That was in the national interest, Mr. Speaker, and we had to provide a Canadian market for Alberta oil in order that the operation could become profitable.
What would now seem to be the problem is the fact that the Canadian government has duties and responsibilities toward all Canadians and it cannot escape them without attracting well deserved criticism.
Therefore it had to take some precautions in the face of such a serious situation and this is the purpose of the bill before us. Moreover, the government should set up a long term energy policy as indicated Thursday afternoon by the Prime Minister to the great satisfaction of all Canadians.
However the establishment of such an overall Canadian energy policy compared to the former one which was partial should not be set up for the second time while ignoring the priority interests of the provinces and mainly of Quebec in this field. The appropriate negotiations will take place between the federal government and the provinces. I hope that all avenues will be explored to ensure adequate supply to the eastern provinces while allowing industrial expansion on their territory.
It is wise to consider two particular points. For the safety of our supplies we must build a pipeline for the transportation of western oil. It is desirable, if possible, that this pipeline be totally located on Canadian soil and be reversible. Here is why: There is currently a crisis, a tension, a war and parleys in the Middle East. Discoveries are made throughout the world, new oil resources are found. A very important one was announced recently in northern Great Britain.
Obviously, the Arabs will be interested in participating in the oil market and in selling their oil at the highest cost possible but they will face competition. The prices will probably settle at a much more normal level than the current prices and will be probably higher than before. But this would enable Canadians if we are still in a position to import from offshore, to save our resources for future generations. Even if we have to ensure safe supplies to all Canadians from Halifax to Vancouver, we have no right to sacrifice at the same time the interests of future generations.
While it is possible and economically feasible to adopt a Canadian energy policy, particularly for oil, to ensure a Canadian market capable of supporting the efficient de-

I believe one should insist on that last part of the Prime Minister's statement so as to allow for the most objective negotiations possible with the Canadian provinces, with the province of Quebec, with the Maritime provinces that invested money and are entitled, if possible, to rely as they have done until now on supplies from the Arab countries, from Venezuela or from any source outside Canada in the coming years.
I would have liked to deal a little longer with the problem as a whole, but there is a detail in the bill that concerns me in a special way and obviously concerns the Quebec people. In Quebec, we are self-sufficient as far as electric energy is concerned. We are more than self-sufficient, we export that energy and have been exporting it for many years; Quebec's hydroelectric system is connected to that of the neighbouring province, Ontario, and billions of kilowatts are delivered by us every year to that province. That same system is connected to the American northeast system. Thus, there is a sort of arrangement and exchange between the systems of those three parts of this continent. The province of Quebec has always been an important source of hydroelectric energy and we have been able, as far as possible, to place it at the disposal of our neighbours the United States and our sister province of Ontario. Of course, we shall continue to do so as far as possible. The province of Quebec still has a large hydroelectric potential to develop; this is already being done and the province is considering even greater projects. I think that as Canadians it is in our interest to encourage the province to make those developments because we will all benefit from it.
But I would like to sound a note of warning to all provinces: the federal government should not take advantage of the situation to assume a right which it does not need. This applies to Alberta as well as to the province of Quebec. I am pleased to find restrictions in the legislation before us, particularly the one year limit, because other-
[Mr. Lessard.l
wise I would not accept it as a Quebecker. Some of my colleagues are in the same position. As members representing various areas of Canada we all are in the same position. Then we should not agree to place it under federal control unless there is a completely new understanding and distribution of powers and responsibilities between both government levels.
So I make that reservation on that basis and I think we should be careful regarding what we intend to do because it might have very serious effects in the years to come. Having made that reservation, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that in the last few weeks the government of Quebec did not seem to have any real policy.
It was thought that Quebec was not aware of the problems it would encounter. Maybe the Quebec leaders did not want to make any big statement which would frighten the population by pointing out the seriousness of the situation, but if you study the statements made during the last week, and particularly if you discuss with certain Quebec politicians, you will realize that these responsible people have nevertheless assembled highly valuable information on the energy situation in general, and in Quebec in particular, and on the choices facing the province.
Some very fundamental questions are being asked by our friends, the Quebec members. A policy has been developed. Yesterday, we outlined the new energy policy. These are the principles established yesterday. There are still many things to do. Such principles have to be analyzed and machinery has to be set up if they are to work out. It is not sufficient to lay down principles. .Mechanisms are needed and have to function under the best possible agreement.
In concluding, I therefore urge all my colleagues to deal with this problem with an open mind, to repress the feelings which we may all have at times when such important issues are at stake. I can assure the House that as a Quebec member, just as much as my colleagues from Alberta who are representing the interests of that province, I am concerned with that problem and I would not want my province to suffer from a federal ruling any more, I think, than our Alberta colleagues would. On the other hand, I am sure that our colleagues from Alberta, like us from Quebec, wish that with good co-operation from provincial governments the best energy policy possible be set up, with regard to the present situation which is urgent, but especially, with regard to Canada's medium and short term needs. Since Providence has endowed Canada with a very advantageous situation in the energy field, if we manage to agree and to set up an objective policy which would be good for all Canadians, we will succeed, Mr. Speaker, in creating here a fantastic economic development. When we consider the difficulties of the European countries, those of our southern neighbour, those of Japan, and when we consider also Canada's long term energy potential, if, through co-operation, we succeed in establishing a policy for a rational development of our energy resources, we will be able to give Canada an important industrial expansion since energy is essential to industrial development. subsubtopic: SUGGESTED GOVERNMENT INVESTIGATION OF FEASIBILITY OF NATIONWIDE PROGRAM FOR PRESERVATION OF HISTORIC SITES AND BUILDINGS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should investigate the feasibility of a nationwide program for the preservation of historic buildings and sites of architectural merit and integrity through financial assistance to municipalities, historical societies and other non-profit organizations for the acquisition, restoration and maintenance of such buildings and sites to be occupied in a manner consistent with original public or private use, but to be open to the public at regular periods.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I move this motion urging a new approach to the preservation of historic buildings and sites. Canada has a rich heritage. It has often been said that to understand a people, to understand a country, one has to understand its history. This is also true if the people of a country as large and diverse as Canada are to understand each other.
It is difficult to understand a country's history without appreciating the actual buildings that the people of earlier generations lived in, their homes, their shops, their places of work, all of which formed part of their character and identity. The carved doors, the old wainscoting, the pine furniture, the fancy brickwork, the iron fences, the stained glass windows-all of these items found in historic buildings tell us something about our forefathers and provide us with that important feeling of continuity with the past.
Canadians know a little more about themselves when they are able to experience historic buildings and sites as part of their daily lives, either at work or in their residential neighbourhoods. For these reasons, I believe the federal government must give a higher priority to the preservation of historic buildings and sites than has been the case to date.
The new approach which I am suggesting would involve much greater participation by private individuals, municipalities, historical societies and other non-profit organizations, not only in terms of money which they might contribute but in the role they might play in the acquisition, restoration, ownership and maintenance of such buildings.
Briefly put, I believe that we should break away from the notion that only government is capable of acting as proprietary trustee for our important historic buildings and sites. Private individuals and organizations are also capable of acting as trustees of our history under certain conditions, yet the present policy of the federal government is to virtually exclude such persons or organizations from participating in federal funding while at the same time maintaining an ownership role. In other words, the general thrust of existing federal programs so far has been based on government ownership. In my view this is not sufficient because it will not permit preservation of a sufficient number of worth-while buildings. My motion today seeks to provide a program which would shift some of the preservation effort and responsibility to the private sector. Since everything today needs a title, I would call it a program for "participation in preservation".
I would not want my remarks today construed as a deprecation of some of the fine work done by the National Historic Parks and Sites Branch of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The important restorations of such historic sites as the Fortress of Louis-burg in Cape Breton, Fort Lennox in Quebec, the Niagara Historic Frontier and Fort George in Ontario, Lower Fort Garry in Manitoba, Rocky Mountain House in Alberta, and Fort Langley in British Columbia have served not only to preserve these sites but to illustrate events in Canadian history to all those who visit these places.

But these types of projects, important as they are, claim the lion's share of the federal budget in this field. They are all grandiose, government-owned and operated projects, reflecting largely military sites or buildings which may create the mistaken impression of Canada as a bellicose nation with a history consisting largely of military events. Also, most of these sites are of significance only to the Anglophone and Francophone groups of this country. Most of the places of historical value to the heritage of the so-called "third group" Canadians have been virtually ignored.
The only site representative of the non-French or nonAnglo aspects of our history which has been considered worthy of full-scale commemoration is the Batoche Rectory in Saskatchewan, the headquarters of the Metis during the great northwest rebellion of 1885 at Duck Lake. The neglect of the contribution of such groups as the Italians, Ukrainians, Jews, Scandinavians and Germans to our heritage not only misrepresents our history but also exacerbates the sense of exclusion felt by these people.
More important, however, these types of projects claim millions of dollars in capital and operating expenses, leaving little if any financial support for smaller buildings which may not be of national historical importance yet which are worthy of preservation to a particular community or neighbourhood. Admittedly, the National Historic Sites Branch does have a limited program under which it can enter into co-operative arrangements with historical societies or municipalities. However, the branch takes on only two or three of these projects each year, and usually to the extent of paying 50 per cent of the cost of acquisition and restoration. The amount of money spent is a mere drop in the bucket compared with the money spent on national historic sites.
For example, in the last fiscal year, 1972-73, the money spent on co-operative agreements was only $87,416, which is only .59 per cent of the total capital and operating expenditures of close to $15 million on national historic sites. In the previous year the amount was only $79,000, or .63 per cent of the total expenditure. That is not to say the branch's program of co-operative arrangement is incapable of accommodating the type of program I have in mind. For example, one of the co-operative agreements involves the restoration of the Grange House in my home city of Toronto. The branch contributed $50,000 to the project owned and operated by the Art Gallery of Ontario which raised close to $600,000 from private sources to complete what is an excellent example of Toronto's early history. Federal participation of this sort happens all too rarely, only two or three times a year throughout the country, an appallingly weak effort. To fit the concept advanced in my motion, the branch's program would have to be expanded a hundredfold, and in certain cases permit participation of private individuals in return for a commitment to maintain and periodically make accessible to the public.
I could suggest any number of historic buildings that could qualify for such a program, buildings which might be irretrievably lost unless action is soon taken. Indeed, one of the excellent initiatives taken by the Historic Sites Branch in 1962 was to establish a Canadian inventory of historic building. This three-phased, ten-year program was the first comprehensive architectural history in the world
Historic Sites
created for a computerized information system. So far the plan has resulted in the recording of the exteriors of over 106,000 buildings across Canada, and the eventual goal is the full restoration of about 700 of those buildings of exceptional significance or architectural merit.
I am proud of the fact that close to 5,000 of those buildings either entered or about to be entered in the computer system are located in an area of my constituency known as the Annex. Several years ago the Annex ratepayers' association, which this year celebrated its fiftieth anniversary, organized a group of volunteers to undertake the task of photographing and recording the details of the many buildings there constructed prior to 1910 and found to be of architectural merit, and in some cases owned by a famous Canadian. Assistance was provided by the Historic Sites Branch through the supplying of proper forms and reimbursement for film. One of the buildings included in the Annex inventory was the residence on Admiral Road of the late Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson when he was a member of the faculty at the University of Toronto. There is another residence on Walmer Road which housed the late Vincent Massey when he was the dean of Victoria College.
Another group of historic houses in the Annex is found in the Huron-Madison area. There is a particular group of nine houses, five of which were constructed prior to 1895 and the remainder before 1905, which last year were threatened with demolition, to be replaced by a high-rise apartment building. At the instigation of the Annex ratepayers' association, the Toronto city council formed a committee, to which I was named, which conducted detailed studies. This committee eventually recommended that a non-profit community corporation be formed to acquire the property now owned by the city for purposes of combined residential-commercial use >n an historic setting. The corporation is now formed and anxiously awaiting CMHC approval of mortgage funding under conditions that will permit about 25 per cent of the historic property to be put to commercial use in order to make the project economically viable. This is a clear example where a federal program of the flexible type which I have proposed would ensure the preservation of these buildings as a supplement to CMHC funding. Alternatively, the CMHC might adopt more flexible guidelines to permit its financing policies to take into account the significant historical element which is a part of this project.
Another building in the Annex worthy of preservation is St. Paul's-Avenue Road United Church, constructed in 1887. It is almost the last visual link with the nineteenth century on that part of Avenue Road, and in only three generations' time it will be older than any building north of the parliament buildings in the entire city of Toronto. The church, because of financial difficulties and a declining congregation, was almost forced to sell out to a development corporation which wanted to erect a high-rise office tower on the site. Fortunately, the officers of the church first sought the advice of the Avenue-Bay-Cotting-ham residents' association and the Annex ratepayers' association, which resulted in the formation of a joint committee and later a non-profit corporation called the St. Paul's Centre Foundation which is now seeking financial assistance in order to lease the church for 30 years for community purposes.

December 7, 1973
Historic Sites
Specifically, the sanctuary of the church boasts the best concert acoustics in Toronto, apart from Massey Hall, and could be easily converted into a first-class hall for the presentation of concerts, plays, recitals, and meetings. Other rooms of the church are ideal for workrooms, classrooms, a drop-in centre and senior citizens' facilities. The church would continue to have facilities for Sunday morning worship and an office for its minister. Again, this is the sort of building which provides a comfortable link with the past for residents of the area and the thousands who drive by it daily. This is the type of project which the federal program I am advocating should encompass. I am sure there are hundreds, even thousands, of buildings in various parts of Canada equally worthy of federal assistance to ensure their preservation.
Just the other day I received in the mail a notice that the old nineteenth century Victoria Opera House in the town of Petrolia, Ontario, where I grew up, was to be restored provided adequate financial assistance could be obtained from private and public sources. That hall had significance for me because it was the place where I entered my first public speaking contest while still in elementary school. The hall and the large building in which it was housed was an important link with the past glories of the nineteenth century which that town enjoyed, and an important part of the learning experience of every child who has grown up there since.
Lest my remarks so far appear to be overly critical of federal government inaction, let me congratulate the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) for having the good sense to establish Heritage Canada, effective last April 2. This is a type of national trust designed initially to involve Canadians in preservation through the sale of memberships at $5 a person. With an endowment of $12 million from the government, this non-profit corporation will be able to generate additional funds from private donations, bequests and membership fees in order to purchase, renovate, sell or lease historic properties of local, regional or national importance.
To a certain extent, the future plans of Heritage Canada may meet some of the objectives of the "Participation in preservation" program embodied in my motion. For example, it is my understanding that Heritage Canada does not intend to make any major purchases of historic buildings, but instead will seek other private agencies or individuals to buy and conserve such properties and then will support them in preparing the property for public use and enjoyment. If Heritage Canada does acquire real property, it may be designated "heritage property" in which case it cannot be sold or mortgaged, but only leased to a government department or agency or private organization under strict conditions. Alternatively, it may be designated merely as a worth-while building, in which case it can be sold or leased for commercial use as a restaurant, boutique, office, residence, and so on and placed under restrictive covenants to protect in perpetuity facades and significant interiors. In the last instance, whole groups of worth-while buildings, indeed whole neighbourhoods of historic significance, may be preserved.
Unfortunately, Heritage Canada is not yet in a position to act. In its August newsletter the corporation indicated

it could not assist in any purchases this year, notwithstanding the risk that some buildings or streetscapes might be irretrievably lost. Moreover, the corporation indicated that it would be obliged to decline all requests for financial help in the restoration of historic buildings in private hands. Only if the property is transferrred to an acceptable public body will Heritage Canada even be in a position to consider requests for support. There is not even any indication of what would constitute an acceptable public body. For example, would the Annex Community Corporation, which will own the nine Huron-Madison houses, or the St. Paul's Centre Foundation, which will lease the church on Avenue Road, qualify under the corporation's directive? Certainly this is far from clear. Obviously, the private individuals who own or lease historic buildings, regardless of their architectural merit and integrity, are going to be denied any assistance.
Heritage Canada may have already fallen into the same rigid philosophy that has characterized the programs of the Historic Sites Branch for so many years. This is a philosophy which says that private individuals are not competent or responsible enough to act as trustees of Canada's historic buildings. Only the government or an acceptable public body can do it. In my view, this is overly paternalistic and is destructive of many of the stated goals of Heritage Canada. Granted, there must be some public protection when government funds are applied to assist a private individual on a restoration project. This protection requires not only a preservation of the historical and architectural integrity of the building, but a check on speculators and unwarranted increases in value accruing to the private owner at public expense. However, this type of problem can be easily overcome through the proper use of restrictive convenants and zoning bylaws.
I was pleased to learn that the government of Ontario has proposed far reaching legislation to permit the province or municipalities to designate historic buildings of provincial or local importance. Moreover, an amendment to the Planning Act would permit municipalities to impose what will be known as "historic conservation district zoning", subject to prior adoption of appropriate policies as a part of the official plan of the municipality. Most important, this legislation will enable municipalities, or the province, through the Ontario Heritage Foundation to make loans or grants to owners or tenants of historic buildings which have been municipally or provincially designated.
There is no paternalism with this program. There is no fear that the private individual will abuse his position of trust as owner or trustee of part of Canada's history. Legislation of this sort is already in place in the province of Alberta, effective May 10 of this year. Legislation similar in nature has been in force in Quebec since 1963, but on a limited basis. Sooner or later some of this philosophy will find its way into the legislative corridors of power in Ottawa. The government cannot do the job alone, particularly in the cities where the pressure of demolition and redevelopment is relentless.
The federal government can leisurely make an inventory of over 100,000 buildings in three years. How many of those buildings have already been destroyed? The government can then make a more complete inventory of one-
December 7, 1973

twentieth of these buildings. How many of those buildings will still be standing? Ten years after the original inventory, the government will select less than 1 per cent of the buildings as deserving of complete restoration, if they can find them. Or will they find only a parking lot or a high-rise apartment building, or an expressway route where once stood a building they decided worthy of restoration?
In a field such as this, in a time such as ours, it is not rational for the government to adopt a "go it alone" policy. The government, the country, cannot afford to spurn offers of aid in this field so vital to our sense of national identity. We must protect and preserve these buildings. The government, now, does not have the resources to acquire and restore all buildings worthy of conservation. They need to encourage, not discourage, attempts by private individuals to act in this field.
Mr. Speaker, I commend to you, to members of this House and to the government my program for "participation in preservation."

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED GOVERNMENT INVESTIGATION OF FEASIBILITY OF NATIONWIDE PROGRAM FOR PRESERVATION OF HISTORIC SITES AND BUILDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join this debate, or discussion really, with the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey). I thank him for bringing forward this whole question and for showing concern and sensitivity for a problem which concerns us all and certainly concerns this government. The hon. member for St. Paul's obviously recognizes the immense strides that have been made by this government in preserving our heritage, more so in the last five or six years than in all its previous history. Much of it is too late, but certainly an immense start has been made.
I really do not think it is fair to say on the one hand that all this had been done, then imply that nothing has been done and suggest that unlimited government funds are available. In all fairness, they are taxpayers' funds and not government funds. I think we must keep things in some sort of perspective here. Hon. members speak about the Annex Historical Society. I think it is an absolutely admirable move on the part of the citizens of that area, as is the North York Historical Society in my constituency and the Unionville group which have done a magnificent job in preserving absolutely exquisite buildings which were built and lived in by the pioneers of that region.
I think the hon. member probably knows, in the village of Unionville, also in my constituency, about the work that is being done by the Unionville Arts Foundation, the historical society and the museum in Markham and places like that. These are local groups which should be encouraged and are being encouraged. I think they well-up from the community; but there is the question of by how much and how far one can legitimately expect the government to go. I should like to see it go as far as it is possible to go, but I think it has gone a long way.
There are a number of trade-offs. For example, we can start talking about Mr. Pearson's home. No one has greater affection for Mr. Pearson than myself, except perhaps Mrs. Pearson. The house has great appeal. But Mr. Pearson lived in many places. One Has to use one's judgment. The same is true with regard to the home of Vincent Massey.
Historic Sites
Do we do the same with the Massey home on Jarvis Street, which is now one of our better restaurants in Toronto? What about all the places where the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) has lived or claims to have lived, visited or was born in? My goodness, it would take up the entire budget. I think we have to watch that.
Coming from Toronto, I could name such places as the old city hall. But which city hall should be preserved, the old one or the old-old one? The old city hall is preserved through the centennial program and it is a treasure of a building. A great preservation job has been done on it. The we have to determine what should be done with what is known as the old city hall at Queen Street. Is it worth preserving? It is typical of a certain type of architecture. In my view it is an ugly type of architecture, but perhaps it is unique and should be preserved. The new city hall will at some time be the old city hall. We have to leave some places for future generations; we cannot have a whole line of city halls along the street. The same problem exists with the Union Station in Ottawa. Ottawans have a deep attachment for it and want to preserve it.
