speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED GOVERNMENT INVESTIGATION OF FEASIBILITY OF NATIONWIDE PROGRAM FOR PRESERVATION OF HISTORIC SITES AND BUILDINGS
speechtext:
Frankly, I question this. I do not think it is a significant building. There is a sentimental attachment to it, but in its usual frugal way the government has converted it into a conference centre for the people of Canada and the international community. There is also the Union Station in Toronto which in its centre part and mezzanine is an example of copied architecture, but a really good one. It was built by an architect of that period. I do not know whether or not it was built by Lennox, as was the old city hall and other well known buildings in Toronto.
We must make a serious decision about what we should preserve and what we should not preserve. Other countries have this problem also. Boston has a particular problem in this respect in trying to keep the city working, the traffic moving and also preserving some rather important sites.
I think the motion is worth while and I compliment the hon. member for covering many points in his comments. However, I would like to refer to my notes to complete the record and to see what has been done. I think it is worth while for all hon. members and for those millions of people who read Hansard regularly from page to page to know precisely what the programs are and what has been done. I must say I speak with a special affection about my own home, which is about 150 years old-but the mortgage still is not paid. It is one of the pioneer homes in the northeast part of Toronto. The Harrison family made the bricks and the glass. They fought with Mackenzie. One of them died in the Upper Canada rebellion, and Mackenzie stayed in it. It is a good thing that we are keeping it in the Liberal tradition.
May I now revert to the policies that have been implemented. The national historic parks and sites of Canada commemorate the persons, places and events which have been declared by the minister, on the advice of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada, to be of major historic or architectural significance in the development of Canada. We have tried to do these things in the context

December 7, 1973
Historic Sites
of what the federal government is trying to do and in the context of its criteria. A policy statement on the national historic sites was tabled in the House of Commons in 1968 by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) on the recommendation of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada. Among other things, the policy elaborated the criteria for the designation of national historic sites for the benefit of parliament and the public.
To be commemorated, a site or structure must be closely associated with a person, place or event of national historical importance, or it must illustrate the cultural, social, political, economic or military patterns of history or of a prehistoric people or archaeological discovery. A building may also be declared of national significance because of its great age or because it is an outstanding example of period architecture of which there are few remaining examples.
This raises the problem of people saying that a site in their town is the one they want to preserve. But should we preserve them all? In advising the minister on the commemoration of places, persons and events of national historical importance, the board may recommend that sites, buildings and other structures of national importance be developed as national historic parks or historic sites, or that commemoration be carried out by the erection of national historic plaques or, in exceptional circumstances, of distinctive monuments. The emphasis, of course, is on national importance, and here we get down to the problem of local groups. We all have them, and there is a great deal of emotion and sentimentality engendered by them. We have the Amswell House in Thornhill, in my constituency, which gained the attention of the press in Toronto on certain days and everyone was concerned. But it was not that unique and it was not of national importance, although it would be nice to have preserved it. I think there is a limit on how far we can go.
Suggestions for the establishment of historic sites and parks come from many sources: the general public, members of parliament, historical societies and other groups, departmental staff, and members of the board themselves. Since its establishment, Parks Canada, on the recommendation of the board, has been instrumental in the creation of more than 80 historic parks and major sites and in the commemoration of some 650 persons and events of national-as opposed to local or regional-significance. Negotiations are at present being conducted with provincial governments for the acquisition of further sites which have been declared to be of major national historical significance.
The facilities of the branch to develop sites of national significance are not such that it is possible to cope directly with the restoration and maintenance of all sites designated as being of national significance and it has, therefore, been a policy of the branch to encourage other levels of government and private organizations to maintain and even restore and operate such structures for the benefit of the public. In this connection, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is empowered to make agreements with other levels of government or with nonprofit, incorporated bodies under which the department may contribute up to 50 per cent of the cost of the acquisi-

tion and restoration of a building of special significance, on the understanding that the other party will contribute the balance of acquisition and restoration costs and will assume all operation and maintenance costs in perpetuity and agree to open the building to the public for a specified minimum period each year. If I understood the hon. member correctly, I do not think he was criticizing those criteria. I think, although there is a case for argument, that they are fair.
The department has entered into more than 30 such cost-sharing agreements with provincial and municipal organizations and with incorporated non-profit societies. An example of the department's involvement in cost-sharing agreements is the Halifax waterfront buildings project in which you, Mr. Speaker, would be particularly interested and which you would appreciate. I am pretty sure your home is among those sites. The project undertaken jointly by the department, by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the city of Halifax and Historic Developments Limited, a Halifax firm of architectural, engineering and civic interests, will undertake the restoration of six historic buildings. Another example is the department's agreement with the Art Gallery of Toronto for the restoration and furnishing of the Grange House in that city, which I believe is the oldest brick house in Toronto, the home of the first governor of Upper Canada, John Graves Simcoe. The building is very attractive and it has been of some utilitarian value.
In addition to the department's activities in the field of historic preservation, acting either solely or in concert with other bodies, a considerable number of such projects have been carried out or are ongoing under the aegis of other federal government departments, provincial or municipal governments and by private interests. Examples are the old Bonsecour market in Montreal, which is a most attractive site, Bastion Square in Victoria, Gastown in Vancouver, and the headquarters in London, Ontario, of a major Canadian company which is still retained as a commercial building. There is the old Bank of Canada building on Toronto Street, which I believe is the head office of Argus Corporation.
An interesting project is the development on Sussex Street, in Ottawa, of one of the old convent buildings as you get down near the Mint, which is being redeveloped for the headquarters of the Department of Urban Affairs. This is a particularly special thing being done in this city and adds to the value of the restoration and preservation of the entire market. These are very special places in Canada that should be maintained. We appreciate them in Halifax, in Charlottetown, in Prince Edward Island, in Quebec City-

speechtext: And in St. John's, Newfoundland, the oldest city in Canada.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED GOVERNMENT INVESTIGATION OF FEASIBILITY OF NATIONWIDE PROGRAM FOR PRESERVATION OF HISTORIC SITES AND BUILDINGS
speechtext:
Yes, particularly so. But one that we seem to forget and that is not getting enough attention is Kingston itself. That city is chock-full of buildings of particular historical and architectural value that could be preserved. In fact, I think the whole city of Kingston should be preserved. I believe that the hon. member for St. Paul's
December 7, 1973

referred to areas of historical significance that should be developed and preserved, and certainly this is one.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED GOVERNMENT INVESTIGATION OF FEASIBILITY OF NATIONWIDE PROGRAM FOR PRESERVATION OF HISTORIC SITES AND BUILDINGS
speechtext: It is coming under provincial legislation.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED GOVERNMENT INVESTIGATION OF FEASIBILITY OF NATIONWIDE PROGRAM FOR PRESERVATION OF HISTORIC SITES AND BUILDINGS
speechtext:
I am delighted that the province is involved and there is room for co-operation with the federal government. In the summer of 1970, Parks Canada launched a nationwide survey of Canada's old structures. Called the Canadian inventory of historic building, the project will take eight to ten years to complete. The program began with the study of building exteriors and will culminate with in-depth studies of the best structures. It is a three-phase program, and as a result we will end up for the first time with an inventory which is properly catalogued and computerized, so that if a local ratepayers' association or historical society wants to preserve a Prince Arthur house, and there are approximately 300 Prince Arthur houses across the country being used for catering establishments, from this inventory we will be able to determine which are the valuable ones to preserve.
This will be the real value of the inventory, because without it we would not know the extent of the architectural heritage we have and of which we should be so proud. This will help preserve our cultural background and soul. When combined with other programs operated by our citizenship branch, and by the Department of the Secretary of State, it will help give us a fuller appreciation of our heritage and history. It is something that is particularly appreciated by our children. The old house in which I live, Mr. Speaker, is a special joy to my children. It gives them an appreciation of certain types of things which they know to be beautiful and assume to be of historic value, things which other people might pass by.
As can be seen from much of what has been said, the federal government is carrying out a number of different complementary programs to identify and preserve sites of national importance. Many provinces and a number of municipalities are also acting to preserve sites of regional and local importance. Despite all this effort, it must be noted that historic preservation is a costly exercise. Unless a structure has been very well maintained, the costs of restoration are high and maintenance is more than normal since in both cases the work must be done to standards of historical authenticity. Not only does this involve research to establish original appearance, but it makes heavy demands on highly trained personnel such as restoration architects and conservators, currently in short supply.
I believe we could discuss this question at much greater length, Mr. Speaker, and I do not think we would be bored by it. It is something in which we all share an interest. I am particularly grateful to the hon. member for bringing this motion forward. I wish the hon. member for North-umberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) were here, because in Cobourg the old opera house is of special importance. I might mention, in passing, the restoration work done on Roosevelt University, on Michigan Avenue in Chicago. It is a rather unique building which was about to be destroyed. It was one of Louis Sullivan's buildings and acoustically was one of the greatest halls in the world. Rather than tear it down, the authorities have preserved it for use as a modern university building and concert hall.
Historic Sites
The hon. member for St. Paul's, who is a lawyer from Toronto, will himself appreciate the value of Osgoode Hall, and Campbell House, named after one of the first chief justices of Ontario. The Law Society of Upper Canada, I believe, paid for its restoration and the moving of it, although I imagine there was some government assistance. Here is a very excellent example of early Georgian, in a Canadian sense, architecture being preserved and moved to the Canada Life property near Osgoode Hall for everybody to see and enjoy. Formerly it was an office building for a jobbers supplier.
These are the kinds of things that local people can do and that we can assist them to continue doing. Some of this work is being done by Heritage Canada, Heritage Ontario, Parks Canada and other such agencies. But it is worth keeping in mind that these things cannot be imposed by the federal government: they have to be done in co-operation with private groups and other levels of government. It is just not good enough to say that the federal government should supply the funds. I am not suggesting that the hon. member is saying that alone, but first there has to be an appreciation and understanding by local authorities and local groups that this work is important. However, there is a limit to these resources, Mr. Speaker. There is a trade-off, about which I spoke.
The fact that this debate is taking place today is somewhat significant. Surprisingly enough, those people who are concerned do read Hansard. Here I refer to the people in government who are concerned with this matter. It is some comfort to them to know that we appreciate their concern and their efforts. All too often they may think that they are working in a vacuum, unappreciated. Here I refer to the people in the National Museums Branch, in Heritage Canada, the National Historic Sites Branch, the NCC, the National Archives-people whose work is appreciated and valued. They do a fine job. They are largely unsung, so I think it is good for them to know that there are a lot of people who support their work and who will support any initiatives they may take or suggest.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will only speak a few minutes, because I see that the hon. member opposite has a few words to say on the matter. I will speak briefly, since I merely want to thank the mover for asking the government and I quote:
. . . the government should investigate the feasibility of a nationwide programme for the preservation of historic buildings and sites of architectural merits and integrity through financial assistance to municipalities, historical societies . ..
Mr. Speaker, I am quite pleased with that motion, because in addition to asking the government to consider the opportunity of establishing a preservation program for historic sites, I have always found-and I think it is good to draw the attention of the House to this-that governments have already acted to preserve our historic sites. However, I have also always found that such action was concentrated in the larger cities: Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg, Halifax, etc. Some thought is always given to the possibility of restoring some historic sites in large cities, but they forget that the entire population is paying for this work.

December 7, 1973
Historic Sites
We do not object to that, indeed, we are even happy about it, but we would like a small share of our tax money to return to our regions. We are asking the civil servants to get out once in a while of our large cities and tbur our areas, because we have marvelous historic sites often maintained by voluntary workers through the efforts of local citizens.
I shall start by drawing the government's attention to a series of centres and historic buildings. We all remember that at the time of the centennial of Confederation, the government asked all social organizations and all cities and municipalities to do something to celebrate that event. In my area we did something. On the occasion of the centennial of Confederation, we erected a building. The government gave us a small grant of about one third the worth of this monument which was meant to be a library. It was eventually turned into a museum, but we are stuck with two thirds of the debt and interests which my constituents must pay, while our requests for assistance from the federal government are left unanswered. And yet, it was mentioned on the application, at their urging, that this building would be a monument to the centennial of Confederation. Even though we still pay taxes for other monuments, we pay taxes on the interests and capital for ours.
If the federal government was prepared to help our area, it could do something to salvage those monuments. Some might blame the authorities of the time for relying too much on the government. Maybe they were overly progovernment and were let down. It would be a fine gesture on the part of the federal government to help pay for those buildings erected to Canada's glory, after all, and to try to set finance afloat, by granting a direct assistance for the maintenance of these buildings, that is the Frangois-Para-dis museum, commemorating a discoverer of my region.
I also draw the government's attention to another well-known monument, that is the Maria Chapdelaine property, that of the famous novelist Louis Hemon, of international reputation, but which was never granted federal aid. This monument was erected to commemorate founders, creators of our region, and I need not say anymore because I believe that Maria Chapdelaine is internationally known. I urge the minister and the federal authorities, if they have any money to spend, to try and help those who are now maintaining this property which needs facelifting. And I believe that this would be a good example of federal co-operation, as well as proof that they really want all parts of this country to be treated the same way. This would help eliminate regional disparities as regards historic sites because our people feel that credits that are voted and taxes that are paid for the maintenance of historic sites are always for purposes of agreements and never for our regions themselves.
I will conclude by referring to another historic monument in my region that is called the Victor Delamarre museum. I believe that the mere mention of his name will remind everyone of the strong man par excellence commemorated by the "Domaine Victor Delamarre" at Bou-chette Lake. Financial assistance has been asked of the federal government for the maintenance of this historical monument. We receive from time to time a little assistance

through local initiatives and opportunities for youth projects, but this is greatly inadequate.
If the government would, once and for all be completely impartial and consider historic sites throughout Canada, then I believe that those I mentioned deserve as much as the others. I have no grudge against Quebec, Montreal, Toronto, or any other city. I only ask the government to be fair, and since everyone pays taxes, they should be equitably distributed. If big cities are proud of their historical monuments, it must be remembered that we are all proud, and we hope to see the day when the government will listen to our voice and help local associations, cities, towns and villages to restore magnificent historical monuments. It would be to the glory not only of the province of Quebec but of the whole of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in a few of the remaining minutes I should like to commend the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) on the resolution that he has placed before the House this afternoon: even though it may be the victim of the usual Friday afternoon experience, I trust he will feel satisfied that this has been a useful and worth-while debate. The hon. member himself admitted that a great deal is being done in Canada with respect to the preserving of historic buildings and sites, and the hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson) sought to spell that out. But it is still true that if we let our history slip away, we will not be able to recover it. I therefore think it is an excellent idea which the hon. member for St. Paul's has placed before the House and before the government, and I hope consideration will be given to it.
I should like in a moment or two to make reference to two projects in which I confess I have a personal interest, but at least I can boast that neither is in my constituency. I mention them because I think they represent the kind of projects in this general area that need to be included.
Sir, and I am thinking of you as Mr. Deputy Speaker, in your province of Nova Scotia there is a great deal of respect for old buildings and places that mark the history of that province. I am particularly interested in a building known as the old meeting-house at Barrington, Nova Scotia. It is a building that was constructed prior to 1800; in fact, back some piece into the 1700s. It is a small but very interesting old building which is now being maintained by the Cape Sable Historical Society. That particular part of Nova Scotia represents a culture and a heritage that is quite different from parts of Nova Scotia 20 or 30 miles away from it. I am familiar with it because it is the part of Canada to which my ancestors came more than 200 years ago and lived in for a long time.
I always find it most interesting to go there and I find that the members of my family, those who came after me, are fascinated by such history as is evidenced just by going into that area. I think an organization such as the Cape Sable Historical Society deserves the kind of support suggested in the motion that is before us. I put forward that building as the type of structure that is different from the monuments, and so on, that were suggested by the last speaker-and as one other branch of our history that
December 7, 1973

should be remembered. I urge that those who are doing their part in this field, as are the members of the Cape Sable Historical Society, should be supported.
The other project in which I am interested is closer to where I now live, although it is not right in my constituency. I refer to the home where my predecessor, the late J. S. Woodsworth, lived for the last number of years of his life. It was for a while the home of my colleague who is not here this afternoon, the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis). Before that it was the home of his father, the Reverend James Woodsworth, who was a very important person in the life of the Methodist Church in western Canada.
We at times think of the homes and birthplaces of those who reached the pinnacle and became premier, prime minister or what have you. Perhaps there are others like the late Mr. Woodsworth whose life should be remembered in this way. There is a society that is getting money together for the purchase of that home and making it a place which people can visit. This is not a commercial. Like the one in Barrington, Nova Scotia, it is a type of building which is perhaps a little different from some of those that have been mentioned.
I take this minute or two to mention these projects for their own sake because I think they are typical of many such projects throughout this country which deserve the kind of support set out in the motion of the hon. member for St. Paul's. Therefore, I commend him for this motion. Perhaps there is no reason why we always have to talk these things out on Friday afternoons. Maybe the group of friendly members who are here would agree to let this motion pass.

That will be about seven times longer than I will have to speak. I commend the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) on this motion. I know he has a sense of history. It was indicated by the hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson), who lives in the Toronto suburbs, that this is because the hon. member now lives in Toronto. I suggest, with respect, it is because of the fact that he lived in Petrolia, Ontario, a very well known place with a sense of history. Every day when you go by the buildings in that community you cannot help being struck by the age of so many buildings. The people there are doing something about preserving them.
I wish private members' hour was two hours, because I could go on for another hour on this subject. I want to mention something that happened in the past which I consider to have been a disaster. The Hon. Alexander Mackenzie lived in the area of Sarnia-Lambton. He was a stonemason and built the county jail, the county courthouse and the county council building prior to the turn of the century. When that building was no longer used by the county council or as a county jail and county courthouse, it was torn down. It was one example of the handiwork of the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie in that area, and it was torn down.
To commemorate the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, we now have an historic plaque which was put in place by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. That department was responsible for doing that. However, how much better it would have been to preserve the ancient county courthouse, jail and county chambers as a memorial to this great Canadian.
We have another building in Sarnia called Lawrence House. It is not as old as some of the buildings in Kingston and Halifax, but it should be preserved. It is my hope that citizens in the Sarnia area will mount an attack to preserve this structure. If it means setting up a non-profit corporation to do so, I hope they will take that kind of action because it is the kind of building that should be preserved.
